When two people, teams, or things are neck and neck, they are so close to each other in a competition or race that it is almost impossible to say who is winning. Neither one has a clear lead. They are essentially tied, matched point for point, step for step.

Think of it this way: if you and your friend are running a race and your shoulders are level with each other — neither of you is ahead — that is being neck and neck.

This idiom was born on the horse racing track, and that origin perfectly explains the image.

In a horse race, when two horses are running so closely that their necks are side by side — literally neck beside neck — it becomes impossible for spectators to judge who is ahead. The neck of a horse is what race officials look at to determine the winner. So when two horses are at the exact same position, their necks are aligned, and the race is too close to call.

Over time, the phrase jumped out of horse racing and into everyday language to describe any situation of extreme closeness in a competition.

The heart of this idiom is closeness and equality in competition. It is not just about being close — it specifically means two sides are so evenly matched that the outcome is uncertain. Neither has a comfortable advantage.
How and When to Use It

You can use "neck and neck" in almost any competitive situation — not just physical races. Here are the main contexts where it naturally fits:

Sports and races:
"The two sprinters were neck and neck for the last 50 metres, and the crowd was going wild."

Elections and politics:
"The two candidates have been neck and neck in the polls all week. Nobody knows who will win."

Business and market competition:
"For years, those two smartphone brands were neck and neck in sales, constantly trying to outdo each other."

Exams, grades, or academic rankings:
"Priya and Arjun are neck and neck for the top rank in their class. It will come down to the final exam."

Games:
"After eight innings, both teams are neck and neck at 3–3. This is going to be a thrilling finish."

"Neck and neck" is almost always used as a predicate adjective — meaning it comes after a linking verb like "be," "remain," or "stay":

  • They are neck and neck.
  • The two runners remained neck and neck until the final bend.
  • The companies stayed neck and neck for months.

You can also occasionally hear it used before a noun, though this is less common:

  • "It was a neck-and-neck race right to the finish." (Here it is hyphenated when used before a noun, as is standard in English.)

This expression carries a sense of excitement and suspense. When you say two things are neck and neck, you are implying that the outcome is still open — anything could happen. The listener automatically understands that the situation is tense and thrilling. It is neither a negative nor a positive expression on its own; it simply describes the state of a very tight contest.

It is important to understand what this phrase does not mean, so you do not misuse it:

  • It does not mean one side is slightly ahead. If someone is winning clearly, you would not say neck and neck.
  • It does not apply to non-competitive situations. You would not say "my two friends are neck and neck in kindness" — it only works where there is a winner and loser being decided.
  • It does not suggest the two sides are identical in all ways, only that their current standing or score is equal at this moment.

Knowing these related phrases will help you understand and use "neck and neck" in a richer context:

  • "Too close to call" — the outcome is so uncertain that no one can predict a winner yet. Very similar in meaning, slightly more formal.
  • "Running even" — progressing at the same pace; less vivid than neck and neck.
  • "Dead heat" — when two competitors finish at exactly the same time or score. This is the result of being neck and neck; a dead heat is what happens at the end when neck and neck competitors finish simultaneously.
  • "Nose to nose" — a less common variant meaning the same thing; again borrowed from horse racing imagery.
A Quick Summary to Lock It In

Neck and neck = two competitors so evenly matched that neither has a clear lead, and the outcome is still uncertain.

Whenever you see a tight, suspenseful competition where no side can be confidently called the winner yet, "neck and neck" is the perfect phrase to reach for.
